triage.name: Enlarged Prostate (BPH)
triage.reason: Older man with lower urinary tract symptoms; diagnosis reachable by history, exam including prostate exam, urinalysis and labs, with retention and prostate cancer as look-alikes.

demographics: Prevalence increases with age; most common prostate condition in men over 50
family_history: BPH in a father or brother

chief_complaints.text: I have to get up several times at night to pee
My urine stream is weak and slow
I have trouble starting to urinate
I feel like I can't empty my bladder completely

hpi.onset: Insidious over months to years; symptoms often ignored until they interfere with daily life
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive lower urinary tract symptoms; nocturia and frequency worsen, and the stream becomes weaker over time
hpi.location: Suprapubic and perineal; urinary symptoms referable to the bladder and urethra
hpi.quality: Hesitancy, weak intermittent stream, and a feeling of incomplete emptying
hpi.severity: Variable; often bothersome enough to disrupt sleep or activities, but may be mild
hpi.timing: Worse at night and after fluid intake before bed; may worsen after caffeine, alcohol, cold medicines, or prolonged sitting
aggravating: Cold or allergy medicines with decongestants

associated_symptoms.text: Getting up multiple times at night to urinate
Urinating more often during the day
A sudden, hard-to-ignore need to urinate
A weak, slow or stop-and-start urine stream
Feeling like the bladder is not emptied completely
Needing to push or strain to get urine out

pertinent_negatives: Bone pain or unexplained weight loss

positives.text: Getting up multiple times at night to urinate
Urinating more often during the day
A sudden, hard-to-ignore need to urinate
A weak, slow or stop-and-start urine stream
Feeling like the bladder is not emptied completely
Needing to push or strain to get urine out

argues_against: Acute one-sided flank pain with blood in urine

atypical.how_it_differs: Diabetic bladder dysfunction and osmotic diuresis can make frequency, urgency, and nocturia more prominent, so the voiding symptoms of obstruction may be overlooked.
Long-standing bladder outlet obstruction may present with fatigue, anorexia, and worsening kidney function rather than prominent urinary complaints.

general.moderate: Comfortable but bothered by urinary frequency; no systemic signs
general.severe: Uncomfortable, may be restless or in visible pain if acute retention; suprapubic fullness may be apparent
general.critical: Distressed with severe pain or uremic signs; may be pale, diaphoretic, or confused if complications develop

findings.maneuver: Perform a digital rectal examination with a gloved, lubricated finger, palpating the posterior prostate
findings.finding: Prostate is symmetrically enlarged, smooth, and rubbery or firm, without discrete nodules

findings.maneuver: Palpate the prostate during digital rectal examination for nodules or induration
findings.finding: No discrete nodule or hard, indurated area

findings.maneuver: Palpate the prostate during digital rectal examination
Inspect and palpate or percuss the suprapubic area
findings.finding: Suprapubic fullness or dullness from a distended bladder, sometimes visibly prominent

findings.maneuver: Test perineal sensation and ask about numbness in the saddle area

labs.caveat: Elevated when chronic urinary retention causes obstructive nephropathy.
May rise with dehydration or renal impairment from obstruction.
Indicates urinary tract infection due to stasis; not part of uncomplicated BPH.
Positive with nitrate-reducing bacteria (e.g., E. coli).

imaging.study: Ultrasound of bladder and prostate with post-void residual
imaging.preferred_when: Initial assessment of bladder emptying and prostate size
Elevated creatinine or suspicion of hydronephrosis
Before surgery or if prostate size affects treatment choice
Hematuria, suspected bladder stones, or prior pelvic surgery

initial.why: Rule out urinary tract infection and hematuria
Screen for prostate cancer in men with >10 year life expectancy; elevated PSA can be from BPH or cancer
initial.only_if: life expectancy >10 years and diagnosis would change management

initial.why: Assess incomplete emptying and risk of retention
initial.only_if: moderate to severe symptoms or suspected retention

supporting.why: Objective measure of urinary flow rate; low peak flow suggests obstruction
Evaluate bladder and urethra for stones, tumors, or stricture
supporting.only_if: hematuria, bladder stones suspected, or prior pelvic surgery
elevated creatinine or concern for chronic retention

not_indicated.why: No role in routine BPH evaluation
Not indicated for routine BPH; may be used if prostate cancer staging is needed
Not routinely indicated unless hematuria and risk factors for bladder cancer

decision_points: PSA should be interpreted in context of prostate size; BPH can elevate PSA
If post-void residual >300 mL, consider urology referral and intermittent catheterization
If hematuria present, evaluate for bladder cancer with cystoscopy and upper tract imaging
If creatinine is elevated, perform renal ultrasound to assess for hydronephrosis

criteria.name: AUA Symptom Index (IPSS)
criteria.summary: Standardized 7-item questionnaire grading storage and voiding symptoms. Total score 0-35: 0-7 mild, 8-19 moderate, 20-35 severe.

differential.name: Prostate cancer
differential.why_considered: Shared lower urinary tract symptoms and an enlarged or nodular prostate on exam.
differential.trigger: Hard nodule or induration on digital rectal exam, elevated PSA, or new bone pain

history: Often asymptomatic early; can have similar voiding symptoms
Bone pain, especially in the pelvis, spine, or ribs (metastatic)
Constitutional symptoms such as unintentional weight loss in advanced disease
Family history of prostate cancer
African American ancestry
exam: Prostate may be nodular, hard, or asymmetrically enlarged, but can be smooth and indistinguishable from BPH
Signs of metastatic disease, such as bony tenderness if advanced
labs: PSA usually elevated, often disproportionately high relative to prostate size; may be normal
Alkaline phosphatase elevated if bone metastases
Urinalysis may show hematuria if locally advanced
imaging: Transrectal ultrasound may show hypoechoic peripheral zone lesion
MRI prostate may show suspicious lesion
Bone scan or PSMA PET if high-risk for metastases

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Irritative voiding symptoms such as frequency, urgency, and dysuria are common with BPH but may be due to infection.

history: Dysuria, frequency, urgency
Cloudy or foul-smelling urine
Suprapubic pain
Fever or chills (if pyelonephritis, flank pain)
May have recent catheterization or instrumentation
exam: Prostate may be tender on DRE if acute bacterial prostatitis
labs: Many WBCs and bacteria on microscopy
imaging: No structural changes typical; may be unilateral hydronephrosis if obstructing stone with infection

differential.name: Overactive bladder
differential.why_considered: Predominant storage symptoms with urgency, frequency, and nocturia, without significant voiding symptoms.

history: Urgency with or without urge incontinence
Frequency and nocturia
No significant hesitancy, weak stream, or incomplete emptying
Symptoms may be triggered by small volumes
imaging: Urodynamic testing shows detrusor overactivity, not obstruction

differential.name: Urethral stricture
differential.why_considered: Weak stream, hesitancy, and incomplete emptying can result from a narrowed urethra, not prostate.

history: History of urethral trauma, instrumentation, or sexually transmitted infection
Symptoms often of shorter duration or following event
May have recurrent UTIs
exam: No significant prostate enlargement on DRE
imaging: Urethrogram shows narrowing at stricture site
Cystoscopy confirms stricture, not prostatic obstruction

differential.name: Neurogenic bladder
differential.why_considered: Similar symptoms, especially in patients with diabetes, neurologic disease, or spinal pathology.

history: Diabetes, spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease, or stroke
May have fecal incontinence or erectile dysfunction
Symptoms may include overflow incontinence
Nocturia may be due to nocturnal polyuria
exam: Neurologic deficits such as lower extremity weakness, sensory changes, abnormal rectal tone or saddle sensation
Prostate may be normal or small
labs: Urodynamic testing shows detrusor underactivity or sphincter dyssynergia
imaging: MRI of spine if suspected spinal cord lesion

differential.name: Prostatitis
differential.why_considered: Urinary frequency, urgency, and perineal discomfort can overlap with BPH.

history: Perineal, suprapubic, or penile pain
Dysuria
Chronic pelvic pain syndrome may have pain with ejaculation
Acute bacterial prostatitis may have fever, chills, and systemic symptoms
exam: Prostate is tender, boggy, and warm on DRE in acute prostatitis
Prostate may be tender in chronic prostatitis
labs: Urine and expressed prostatic secretions show leukocytes and bacteria in bacterial prostatitis
PSA may be elevated but transient
Urine culture positive in acute bacterial prostatitis
imaging: Usually normal; may have prostatic abscess on transrectal ultrasound if not responding

severity.mild: AUA symptom score 0–7; symptoms are intermittent and not bothersome; no significant post-void residual; normal renal function; prostate may be enlarged but no complications.
severity.moderate: AUA symptom score 8–19; bothersome symptoms, especially nocturia and frequency; post-void residual 100–300 mL; no urinary retention or renal impairment; no recurrent UTIs.
severity.severe: AUA symptom score 20–35; marked bother, severe nocturia, weak stream; post-void residual >300 mL; may have recurrent UTIs, bladder stones, or early renal impairment; risk of acute urinary retention.

red_flags.finding: Complete inability to urinate with painful bladder distension
red_flags.meaning: Acute urinary retention; requires immediate catheterization.
Pyelonephritis or urosepsis; needs urgent evaluation and antibiotics.
Could indicate bladder cancer, stones, or severe BPH; cystoscopy indicated.

red_flags.finding: New saddle anesthesia or leg weakness
Bone pain, especially in the back or hips
red_flags.meaning: Metastatic prostate cancer; needs PSA and imaging.

red_flags.finding: Elevated creatinine with hydronephrosis on imaging

complications.name: Acute urinary retention
clues: Precipitated by decongestants, alcohol, or surgery

special_populations.differences: Symptoms are more prevalent and may be complicated by comorbidities; anticholinergic medications worsen retention; cognitive impairment may mask symptoms until acute retention occurs.
Diabetic cystopathy can cause detrusor underactivity, making symptoms and post-void residual worse; elevated glucose increases osmotic diuresis and nocturia.
May present with uremic symptoms rather than urinary complaints; need prompt bladder drainage if obstructive nephropathy suspected.

key_questions.question: When did these urinary symptoms start, and how have they changed over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset and slow progression over months to years

key_questions.question: Do you have trouble starting to urinate?
Is your urine stream weak, slow, or stop-and-start?
Do you feel like your bladder does not empty completely after you urinate?
How many times do you wake up at night to urinate?
key_questions.looking_for: Nocturia, typically two or more times per night

key_questions.question: How often do you urinate during the day?
Do you have a sudden, strong urge to urinate that is hard to postpone?
Do you have any pain or burning when you urinate?
key_questions.looking_for: Dysuria absent in uncomplicated BPH; its presence suggests UTI or prostatitis

key_questions.question: Have you ever seen blood in your urine?
key_questions.looking_for: Gross hematuria, which warrants evaluation for bladder cancer and other causes

key_questions.question: Have you ever been completely unable to urinate, even though your bladder felt full?
Do you have fever, chills, or flank pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Signs of urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including any over-the-counter cold or allergy medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: Decongestants, antihistamines, anticholinergics, or diuretics that can worsen symptoms

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, a stroke, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, or a spinal cord problem?
key_questions.looking_for: Neurologic or metabolic causes of bladder dysfunction

key_questions.question: Have you had prior urinary tract infections, urinary catheters, or prostate surgery?
Has anyone in your family had BPH or prostate cancer?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of BPH or prostate cancer

key_questions.question: How much caffeine and alcohol do you drink, especially in the evening?
key_questions.looking_for: Evening caffeine or alcohol intake that worsens nocturia and urgency

key_questions.question: Do you have any new weakness in your legs, numbness in your groin or buttocks, or trouble with bowel control?
Do you have any new bone pain, especially in your back, hips, or pelvis, or unexplained weight loss?
Do you have difficulty getting or keeping an erection, or pain with ejaculation?
key_questions.looking_for: Erectile dysfunction may coexist; pain with ejaculation can occur with BPH or prostatitis

reasoning_points: Older man with gradual onset of both voiding and storage lower urinary tract symptoms
Voiding symptoms: hesitancy, weak intermittent stream, and incomplete emptying
Storage symptoms: urgency, frequency, and nocturia
Smooth, symmetrically enlarged, non-tender prostate on digital rectal examination
No discrete nodule or induration to suggest prostate cancer
Normal urinalysis without evidence of urinary tract infection
Elevated post-void residual volume supports bladder outlet obstruction
Normal or mildly elevated PSA consistent with BPH after considering age and prostate size
Renal function normal, or if abnormal, associated with obstructive nephropathy and hydronephrosis
Alternative causes such as UTI, prostate cancer, urethral stricture, and neurogenic bladder considered
AUA symptom score quantifies symptom severity

easy: Classic older man in his 60s with months of nocturia, frequency, and weak stream
Smooth symmetrically enlarged prostate without nodules
medium: Patient with bothersome urgency and mild dysuria, so UTI must be ruled out first
PSA moderately elevated, requiring prostate cancer risk assessment
Diabetes mellitus or use of anticholinergic medication complicates symptom interpretation
Recurrent UTIs from chronic incomplete emptying
hard: Presents with acute urinary retention after taking a decongestant
Older man with fatigue and elevated creatinine from long-standing obstructive nephropathy
Predominant nocturia in a diabetic patient with poor glycemic control, where neurogenic bladder and osmotic diuresis confound BPH symptoms
Gross hematuria requiring cystoscopy and upper tract imaging to exclude bladder cancer
Hard prostate nodule on exam raising suspicion for prostate cancer
